technique: entering mid-action, with no setup at all
lesson:
Today we work on one technique. It's starting a poem already inside an action, with no explanation first. The poem does this with its very first words. It opens "The one ash left standing by the stone wall." No one tells you where you are or why. The tree is just there. Later it does it again: "all week the tending ran on without you." You get the action without the backstory. And at the end: "go wake the quiet and let it fill." A command, no lead-up.

Here is why this works on you. When a poem skips the setup, you have to catch up while it moves. That keeps you paying attention. You feel dropped into something real instead of prepared for it.

Try this: write your first line as if you are halfway through a sentence you already started.

The second time, listen for how much the poem never explains.

Here is the poem, twice.
poem:
The one ash left standing by the stone wall
has dropped its leaves and its keys both at once—
bare a week early, the way ash goes, sudden,
while the oaks down the line still hang on rust.
It stands there spent and done with its giving.
You know the feeling, a little: all week
the tending ran on without you, quiet work
that squares to the cent when a man keeps at it,
the small accounts of care that mend somewhere else—
a word set down soft where someone's hurting,
a thing made right behind its own locked door.
The pile out back is a hand shorter now,
the stove banked low and the first real cold come in.

The kettle's just a match-strike away from warm—
go wake the quiet and let it fill.
